item.title: California sues OpenAI, alleging it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman speaks at an event in San Francisco. (Heather Diehl / Getty Images) California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology. California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta’s office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT “misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public.” Bonta’s office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” He said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a “framework for additional identification and disclosure” of unintended activity, and will “continue to engage” with Bonta’s office “to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a “warning shot” and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents. Bonta’s office said the company’s “disregard for the public safety” created a “public nuisance” in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in “unfair” or “fraudulent” practices. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said. The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined. The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections. The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society. OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company’s website that its “first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity” and in a way that empowers “people broadly,” not just a concentrated few. “We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem,” they wrote. They went on to say that “AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions.” They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. “The goal wasn’t to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use,” they wrote. The company called the Hugging Face attack “evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.” Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta’s office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” but the scope of the problem isn’t fully known because OpenAI hasn’t answered “detailed questions” about them. In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure. Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors . Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release. “This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated,” OpenAI said in a statement. Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should “pass off the blame to machines” while letting those who create them escape accountability. “The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions,” Bonta said at a news conference Monday. “Whether it’s a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don’t build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards,” he said. Bonta’s office said it is encouraging “anyone with information relevant to this case” to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report . He said his office is also watching other AI companies “closely,” but declined to elaborate. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/california-sues-openai-alleging-endangered-184249420.html

item.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex-CEO
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year [Getty Images] Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley [Reuters] New rules The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad . The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent. But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors. Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns. But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. While Singapore does not necessarily prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Advanced semiconductors, crucial for the development of AI models, are at the centre of the US and China's technological rivalry. US officials have long viewed the country's technological supremacy as a matter of national security and have expressed concerns that sharing the best chips could give China's economy and military a boost. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said. The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. 'A handshake with Jensen' Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question." But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine". Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm. Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading. In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang". Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation. For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday. Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? item.title: Ex-Commerce Dept. staffers say there was a lack of enforcement under Lutnick
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of highly sensitive computer chip smuggling. A key national security responsibility of the department is investigating and enforcing bans on the export to China and other U.S. adversaries of advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated weapons. "There was an inexplicable refusal to use the tools at their disposal for national security over the last year," one former Commerce official told CBS News. Scrutiny of Lutnick's tenure has heightened in recent days with Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of spying, calling it "an attempt to smear China." As the scandal has unfolded, senior officials and members of Congress have questioned how Nvidia was permitted to sell chips to companies with deep ties to China, and whether the Commerce Department policed those exports effectively. The answer, according to some of Lutnick's former staff, was not at all. Four ex-Commerce officials spoke with CBS News, asking to remain anonymous, fearing professional reprisals for discussing their recent experience in government. "We weren't able to add entities to the Entity List. That was just a complete stop," one former Commerce employee said, referring to the federal list of firms that the U.S. government has banned from buying the most advanced chips due to the belief they would route them to China or other adversaries. Another former Commerce official said a whole year passed with no companies added to the list, noting that this was the first time that had happened in 18 years. The Federal Register shows the last time entities were added was Oct. 9, 2025, and the last yearlong gap in additions was in 2008. The first former staffer said the agency's own enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips had been delivered, but that Commerce directors allegedly took no action. Placement on the list triggers more stringent license requirements and creates a higher threshold to prevent sensitive products from getting where they shouldn't, the ex-official said. Instead, "nothing happened," the ex-official said. The Biden administration issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023, and in January 2025 issued an interim final rule to block China and other adversaries from obtaining the most advanced AI chips, both directly and through third-party countries. In May 2025, President Trump's Commerce Department rolled back the rule, arguing it "would have stifled American innovation." Instead, the department said it would strengthen export controls for AI chips by issuing guidance to the industry and public. There are growing signs that bans on exporting advanced U.S. computer chips have been circumvented in large quantities, according to published reports. An April 2026 study by AI research nonprofit Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025, comprising "roughly a quarter of the comput[ing power] China acquired through legal channels or domestic production." Tech news site The Information reported that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips allegedly ended up with Chinese companies since 2023 just through companies linked to Alice Huang , the suspected Chinese agent accused of an affair with Nvidia's ousted CEO. The report cited sources close to her for the estimate. And a former researcher at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, published a paper last week claiming to have found digital forensic evidence that top Chinese AI models were trained using Nvidia chips banned in China. One former Commerce staffer described the department under Lutnick as "very chaotic, very frantic," with staff sometimes learning of major policy changes via media reports, including a pivot to allow the sale of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China — the company's second-most advanced tier of GPUs. "We found out about that in The New York Times," the ex-Commerce official said. "It was pretty clear that the decision was made between Trump and Jensen Huang." The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment. CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment. On Monday the department imposed a new rule requiring licenses for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand, aimed at closing a loophole through which chips were exported to China via an intermediary. But the Commerce Department suggested that its own involvement was limited, describing the rule as "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers." The department lost two of its most senior and experienced experts shortly after Lutnick took office. One was Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration. Borman had been with the department for over 30 years. Another veteran official, Eileen Albanese, was let go from her longtime role as director of the Office of National Security Controls. Reuters first reported their departures in February 2025, the same month Lutnick started running the department. "They kicked off the administration by essentially firing the two most respected people," said one former employee. A profile on the website of law firm Akin Gump, where Albanese now works, says she played a "key role in the development of U.S. export control policy and regulations for advanced artificial intelligence chips and semiconductor manufacturing tools." "Matt and Eileen were treasures of the U.S. government," one former Commerce staffer said. Albanese did not respond to a request for comment. Borman declined to comment. Former officials said subsequent changes under Lutnick helped prompt an "exodus" of up to 50 skilled staff members over the past 18 months. Over time, those who departed were among the most experienced officials who dealt with key areas including chips and export control enforcement, the ex-staffers said. "It was an exodus of the finest engineers and scientists, the key experts on AI, on Russia, on diversion, our key expert on chips. Decades of institutional memory and skill went out," an ex-employee said. Key roles remain vacant in Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the department in charge of export controls, according to a registry of current senior federal employees. The principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, the same role for export enforcement and the chief of staff roles are all currently unfilled, the records say. Some staff described a bottleneck at the Bureau of Industry and Security, accusing its chief — Jeffrey Kessler, a top deputy to Lutnick — of "micromanaging" and blocking enforcement against companies suspected of smuggling chips. "He made everything go through him. Literally every possible decision, the most minor things. It's impossible for one person to manage that level of things," one former employee under Lutnick told CBS News. "He didn't want to make any decisions on his own. He would want you to make a memo and he would say, 'Package it up with options for me to bring to a decision maker,' which always cracked me up. Because it's like, who are you? A concerned citizen?" "The career workforce felt frustrated and stymied," said one former staffer from the previous administration, who is close to many who remained in the department. "They felt like they were unable to do their jobs because [Kessler and Lutnick] were standing in their way." The former staff members told CBS News that the critical view of Lutnick and his deputy was widely shared in the department. Cabinet members have even voiced criticism, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen t telling CNBC last week that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department and others in the administration. "Commerce has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told the channel. "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above" a certain sophistication, Bessent said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/howard-lutnick-commerce-department-chips-chaos-former-employees/

item.title: 'Everybody's shell-shocked': GOP insiders face 2028 prospects after midterm defeats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On Election Day, many Republicans were bracing for a tough outcome, but not what has been described as a blue tsunami. "I thought that we were going to keep the Senate," former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel told ABC News. "I didn't think that Democrats could make inroads in states like South Carolina and Kansas and even Texas." Joe Raedle/Getty Images - PHOTO: RNC Chairwoman Ronna McDaniel delivers remarks before the NBC News Republican Presidential Primary Debate, Nov. 8, 2023, in Miami. Democrats did more than make inroads. They flipped eight GOP-held Senate seats and as of Monday, Democrats hold 256 House seats to the GOP's 170. There are still some outstanding races as of Monday: nine House races and one Senate race. Over a dozen Republican donors and operatives told ABC News that the Republican Party is still in shock after the sweeping midterm losses. They pointed to a message that focused on culture wars and failed to reach voters squeezed by costs tied to the war in Iran and a Latino coalition that slipped away. Some argued Vice President JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee. Vance, who has not formally announced he is launching a presidential bid for 2028, has acknowledged "there's a chance" he won't run in 2028. 'The South is in play': Longtime red states emerge as potential battleground for Democrats The president’s record- low approval ratings were also difficult to ignore, some said. "The losses are all about Trump," said one Republican consultant who worked on races out West and spoke to ABC News on the condition of anonymity. "This was a total rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his politics." RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement that Republicans will "continue to put America first,” highlighting that the RNC raised $130 million, sending more than $60 million directly to Republican campaigns. When reached for comment, the White House emphasized Trump’s signature tax legislation and said that Trump will continue to work for the American people. "Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, secured the border, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals. President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told ABC News in a statement. Vance's office, when asked for comment, deferred to the White House. A m ess a ging p roble m The donors and operatives who spoke to ABC News agreed Republicans lacked a clear message on affordability -- a key issue for voters. "We need to talk about pocketbook issues. We didn’t do that,” said Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, a group that fundraises for moderate Republicans. Mike Blake/Reuters - PHOTO: Supporters react at a midterm election night party for Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton in Garden Grove, Calif., Nov. 3, 2026. T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist who worked on Republican Darline Graham’s Senate race, said Democrats were talking about affordability "in a more tangible way than we were … We have conservative solutions to these issues, we just didn’t deliver." A GOP strategist involved in many 2026 races said the party's turnout operation will likely take much of the blame. ABC News' analysis of early voting in Texas and Georgia a week before Election Day showed greater Democratic enthusiasm. "We just weren't hitting the numbers we needed to hit of just sheer Republicans voting. A lot of them stayed home, and we knew that was happening," the strategist said. Tom Brenner/Getty Images - PHOTO: Attendees react to election results confirming the results projecting Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico as the winner during a midterm election night watch party, Nov. 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The Republican consultant who worked on races out West added that Republicans had "no choice" but to run on culture war issues because of the high costs brought on by the Iran war. "You can't tell people to ignore your lying eyes,” the source said. "[Republicans] had no choice but to go down the culture-war road because we couldn't talk about the economy." Trump said in a phone interview with Fox News on election night that he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm results and added that part of the reason was the Iran war, directly linking it to gas prices. In a social media post after the election, Trump wrote that Republicans would have been more successful had he been on the ballot. Revers a l a m ong L a tino voters According to the ABC News Voter Poll, in 2026, Latino voters nationally supported Democratic House candidates by a 30-point margin. In 2024, it was a 13-point margin. Trump acknowledged his mass-deportation policies may have been "too tough" in an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes" after the midterms. Mike Madrid, a GOP consultant who studies Latino voting behavior, said "there is no question that the ICE stuff and deportations played a role." "There’s also no question that the economy was the No. 1 factor. But in some districts, like south Texas, they're one and the same. Immigration is the economy there," Madrid said. Latino vote helped thwart Texas Republicans' redistricting effort Democrats swept every congressional district along the southern border, flipping several Republican-held seats in Texas. Billionaire donor John Catsimatidis told ABC News that the losses came down to the war in Iran and "ICE being too tough on waiters and busboys." Immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has reached local businesses and restaurants. A BC News reported l a st M a y that in D.C., federal law enforcement officials visited dozens of restaurants, carry-out spots and bars across several neighborhoods. A fight over who le a ds the RNC RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie announced on Nov. 5 that she's challenging RNC Chair Joe Gruters, saying the party should "be willing to confront where we fell short." A source close to Gruters confirmed to ABC News that he is running for reelection. Alex Wong/Getty Images - PHOTO: Republican National Committee (RNC) Chairman Joe Gruters uses a giant gavel to mark the start of the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. While Trump has since reaffirmed his support for Gruters, some Republicans questioned Gruters' competence. “Joe Gruters failed the Republican Party, and I find it puzzling that he believes he deserves to be reelected,” said an RNC member. Florida GOP Chairman Evan Power said in a statement, however, that "Gruters was a key partner in our fight to keep the Free State of Florida red, and he’s the leader I trust to keep our party on offense and ready to win in 2028." McDaniel said "the committee should support whoever the president wants to be the RNC chair." She added that donors who may be discouraged from giving in the future need an autopsy from the party over what went wrong. "People are still wondering what happened, and the sooner that a plan is put forward, and they get in the field and they get data … That's going to be what’s going to bring donors back. But right now, I think everybody's shell-shocked." The ro a d to 2028 While Vance hasn't ruled out a run in 2028, some donors told ABC News that his proximity to Trump may be a liability. But a Vance ally who spoke to ABC News cautioned against writing off Vance, comparing it to the 2016 and 2024 election cycles, when different parts of the Republican Party wrote Trump off. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo - PHOTO: Vice President JD Vance speaks during a National Veterans' Small Business Week event, Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington. And although Vance is still undecided about a 2028 presidential run, many of Vance's allies expect that he will run for president in 2028, sources confirmed to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl. Vance's allies say he will decide whether to pursue a White House bid on his own timeline. But some Republicans see an opening for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028 following the midterm elections. Rubio has said he has no plans to run for president in 2028, adding that he would support Vance if he mounted a presidential run. Catsimatidis said his family has been supporters of Vance, but he has known Rubio for 15 years and considers the nomination "still open." A Texas-based GOP donor said the next nominee must appeal to "most all Republicans, a majority of independents and a reasonable group of conservative Democrats." "We're in like stage two with a five-stage model of grief or something. We're not at the writing-checks-for-new-people yet stage," said one donor. "America doesn't want more MAGA." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/everybodys-shell-shocked-republican-operatives-face-2028-prospects/story?id=138117916

item.title: Ground stop chaos spurs fight in Congress over air traffic control funding
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – Congress is under pressure to act after air traffic control issues grounded flights nationwide last week , setting up a new funding fight on Capitol Hill and further complicating lawmakers' efforts to avoid another government shutdown before Christmas. Trump administration officials are pleading for billions of additional dollars to modernize what they acknowledge is an aging system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he's asking lawmakers to fast-track a $50 billion package to prevent further communications malfunctions like the one that derailed air travel before the weekend. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are already voicing skepticism about the request, with Democrats pointing to unused Federal Aviation Administration funds and Republicans balking at the topline number. Despite those concerns, there's a near-universal understanding on Capitol Hill that the FAA's systems are in desperate need of a revamp. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, indicated on CNN over the weekend that while Congress has "given the administration what they asked for," there could be an openness to additional spending. "If they need more, they should come up and justify it," he said. "I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system." Read more: Sean Duffy blames switchover in Arkansas for FAA's ground stop Equipment 'heart attack' The new funding request could quickly become another variable in the ongoing negotiations to avoid another shutdown after Dec. 11, when government funding is set to run out. Several Senate Democrats have signaled a willingness in recent weeks to risk a shutdown to pressure President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran . According to federal officials, the air travel meltdown that disrupted Americans' lives and stranded them at airports was caused by a breakdown in the FAA's communications network. It was prompted by the replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas , as part of an ongoing effort to switch out old copper wires with fiber-optic cable. Trump and those around him have since blamed the problem on outdated technology. "I have systems that are from the '90s. I have radar that are from the '60s and '70s," Duffy said on CNN before emphasizing a need for more funding. Trump weighed in on the situation for the first time Nov. 16. "Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," the president told reporters. He said he was "sure" Congress would soon send more dollars to the FAA. Duffy to meet with Senate GOP Duffy is expected to sit in on Senate Republicans' weekly lunch on Nov. 17, where he'll continue to make the case for his funding request. As of Nov. 16, he had not released comprehensive details on how the $50 billion request would be spent. Before upping his ask, however, Duffy spent the last few months pitching an initial $30 billion. Sen. John Kennedy, R-Louisiana, who told USA TODAY he'd be supportive of appropriating more money, said he wasn't sure why the request increased "overnight." "I understand we have inflation, but it's not that dramatic," he said half-jokingly. "They just need to do a better job of explaining it to us." Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, expressed the same sentiments, saying "people have got to explain to me really even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion." Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he, too, wanted clarification. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," he told reporters. Senate Republicans more broadly have already "attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being addressed." Democrats skeptical of unspent funds Democrats are signaling an early frustration with Duffy's request. They've spent the last few days pointing to a $12.5 billion allocation in Trump's so-called "One Big, Beautiful Bill" meant specifically for air traffic control system upgrades. According to Washington Rep. Eric Larsen, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, $11 billion of that remains unspent. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, called Duffy's funding ask a "$50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver." "Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner," she said in a statement. "Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner." Some Republicans have similar questions. "They have funds available, near as I can tell, that have not been contracted," said Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, adding he has questions for Duffy about "why they haven't spent the money they've got." Duffy has defended the Transportation Department, saying all of that tranche of money will be spent and deployed by the end of 2028. None of the money Congress included in that batch of funding, he argued, could go toward fully replacing new telecommunications architecture. "They were very specific on how we spend the 12.5, and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build," Duffy said on ABC News . "They need to give me additional money to finish that project." Transportation Department and FAA staff will brief congressional staffers about the latest funding request this week. item.title: Trump floats meeting with Kim Jong Un that could give North Korean leader a win
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Holland, Gram Slattery and David Brunnstrom WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, an announcement that could dramatically reshape his trip through East ‌Asia. The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 first term in unprecedented direct diplomacy that failed to persuade ‌Kim to give up his nuclear weapons. Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting during his current term, but also previously previewed meetings with Kim that never took place, including during ​a trip to Asia last year. Senior US officials have previously said he has no immediate plans for another meeting, while North Korea has said it sees no need for talks at this time and denounced hostile US policies. Trump told reporters while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader's presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. "(Xi) was here ... and we're also going ‌to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet ⁠with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said. "So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot." Trump added in reference to Kim: "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi." North Korea's mission to the United Nations did ⁠not respond to a request for comment on Trump's remarks. The Kremlin said on Monday a planned meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi on the sidelines of this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China would have a major impact on global affairs. Trump said he would discuss denuclearization, Iran and Ukraine with Xi and Putin, as ​well ​as trade and the economy, but US officials and analysts have played down the ​possibility of a meaningful agreement emerging. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted ‌Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying later on Monday that Putin could meet Kim if he comes to China. North Korea has sent about 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia's war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion. Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington's Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, said Trump's comments made clear he had asked Xi to bring Kim to China for a meeting. "One could see a huge diplomatic victory for Kim if he were to share a ‌stage with the US, Russia, China ... the three other nuclear powers in Asia - in ​addition to any bilateral with Trump," he said. "The common narrative is that China would not ​want to distract from their hosting APEC but I think Xi’s ​global diplomacy offensive would probably be enhanced, in his mind, if he were bringing together all of the leaders for ‌this extraordinary meeting," Cha said. Trump's interest in renewed engagement with ​Kim comes seven years after their last ​summit ended without agreement when they failed to bridge differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons and sanctions relief. Since then, North Korea has significantly expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities while strengthening ties with Russia and China, and any willingness by Trump to make major concessions to ​Pyongyang risks creating friction with regional allies. Trump has referred ‌to North Korea as a nuclear power, a status allies in the region and the West have refused to recognize despite ​the dozens of nuclear warheads experts believe Pyongyang has built. (Reporting by Steve Holland and Gram Slattery; Additional reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt and ​David Brunnstrom; Editing by David Ljunggren, Nia Williams, Caitlin Webber and Lincoln Feast.) item.title: Poll shows that 35% of Trump voters skipped the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump (AP) New survey results show that 35% of President Donald Trump's 2024 voters didn't cast a ballot in the midterm elections. The findings suggest Republicans' crushing losses this month were driven largely by Trump supporters staying home rather than abandoning the GOP for Democrats, according to a new J.L. Partners analysis reported by the New York Post . The pollster found that low Republican turnout accounted for 10 percentage points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, while voters switching parties accounted for the remaining five points. Just 8% of Trump's 2024 supporters voted for Democrats on Nov. 3. "The GOP should not throw the MAGA baby out with the bathwater just yet," J.L. Partners founding director James Johnson said, the Post reported. "If Republicans can energize their 2024 vote in 2028, then they may yet have a shot at winning again." The analysis, based on an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters and more than 30,000 campaign interviews, found particularly steep turnout declines among key segments of Trump's coalition. Among his 2024 supporters, 46% of those without college degrees failed to vote, along with 44% of those older than 65 and 39% of rural voters. Johnson said the turnout collapse alone would have cost Republicans control of Congress, even without voters switching parties. "Even without a single voter switching, the GOP would have lost the Senate and House," Johnson said. The findings bolster Trump's argument that Republicans suffered because he wasn't on the ballot. However, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis suggested GOP voters stayed home because they were dissatisfied with congressional Republicans' performance. "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," DeSantis told Fox News. The survey also found potential vulnerabilities for Democrats heading into 2028. Nearly half of Democrat voters, 48%, said their midterm vote was primarily against Trump rather than in support of Democrat policies. Only 30% of registered voters believed Democrats have a viable presidential candidate for 2028. Meanwhile, CNN reported that Trump's declining popularity remains a significant obstacle for Republicans. CNN's voter polling found that 86% of Americans who disapproved of Trump's performance backed Democrats in House races. Cost of living emerged as the leading concern across every demographic group in the J.L. Partners survey. Johnson suggested the Iran war contributed to voter frustration over rising prices, particularly gasoline. The survey's overall margin of error was 3.4 percentage points. Despite the GOP's losses, Johnson said the results indicate Republicans could rebound by rebuilding turnout among Trump's 2024 supporters rather than abandoning the political coalition that returned him to the White House. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: FEMA will test a nationwide emergency alert on Tuesday. Your phone won't get it.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Be forewarned: On Tuesday afternoon, TVs and radios — not wireless phones — nationwide will blare a jolting emergency alert. But don’t be alarmed; it’s only a test. We repeat: It’s only a test. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), along with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), is running the test to ensure the Emergency Alert System (EAS) for radio and television works during an actual emergency, such as a natural disaster, terrorist attack or other threat to public safety. Wireless phones will not receive the test alert. “Wireless Emergency Alerts were tested in 2023, but they will not be part of this year’s test,” according to FEMA. It comes amid online conspiracy theories that there will be a 90-day power outage on Tuesday, Nov. 17, particularly following last week’s Microsoft global Outlook outage and the Federal Aviation Administration’s rare ground stop. The federal government has not announced a nationwide 90-day blackout or plans to shut down the U.S. power grid. The rumors are centered around a Pentagon plan to ensure the military has access to critical energy, infrastructure and other resources in case of future disruptions. Here’s what you can expect and what to know about the FEMA test on Tuesday. When will the alert test happen? The nationwide test is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 17, at approximately 2:20 p.m. ET. Here’s when you can expect to be alerted depending on your time zone: 2:20 p.m. ET 1:20 p.m. CT 12:20 p.m. MT 11:20 a.m. PT 10:20 a.m. AT 9:20 a.m. HT What will the test look and sound like? Radio and television broadcasters nationwide will interrupt their programming with a message that generally says: “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.” According to FEMA , the Emergency Alert System involves thousands of independently operated radio, television, cable, satellite and wireline broadband providers. Since they use different equipment, the visual or audio formats may differ by station. “The test will include alert tones to support accessibility for individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing,” according to FEMA. And depending on the broadcaster and their capabilities, the message will be delivered in English, Spanish or both. How long will the test last? If your TV or radio is on and tuned to a broadcast station, cable system, satellite radio or television provider, or wireline video service, you should receive the test from the EAS, which is expected to take about one minute. Why is the national emergency test happening? Federal law requires FEMA to test the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) at least once every three years. The last national test was conducted on Oct. 4, 2023. “If an actual emergency or significant weather event occurs on test day, FEMA and the FCC may postpone the test,” according to FEMA . “The backup date for the nationwide test is December 3, 2026.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/fema-will-test-its-emergency-alert-system-tomorrow-heres-what-to-expect-210358652.html

item.title: Mayor Mamdani to disband controversial NYPD protest unit, fulfilling promise
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, or SRG, after months of discussions, officials announced Monday. "What we're doing today is announcing the disbanding of the Strategic Response Group and announcing a completely new approach to how we treat protest in our city," Mamdani told Eyewitness News in an exclusive joint interview with the NYPD Commissioner. The SRG is the NYPD's citywide rapid-deployment force that specializes in counterterrorism but also responds to major crimes and mass demonstrations. Critics have argued that the unit's crowd-control tactics are heavy-handed and provocative. Tisch said the SRG's 500 highly trained, uniformed officers will be reassigned, with many moving to the department's Counterterrorism Bureau. When asked whether the move represented a compromise, Tisch said, "No, I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers. And over the past year, we have made a number of massive changes in the department that strengthen our counterterrorism efforts, this among them." Mamdani said the city's new approach will focus on reducing tensions during demonstrations. "In addition to separating out those responsibilities, we're also emphasizing an approach of de-escalation, an approach of dialogue," he said. Over the next year, the city plans to hire and train civilians to work with protest organizers before and during demonstrations. Tisch said the change will not affect how the NYPD responds to civil disorder. "Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions, like, for example, the celebrations following the Knicks' epic championship," Tisch said. "And so New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to." The commissioner had previously reduced the use of the SRG at protests while stopping short of disbanding the unit. The move fulfills a campaign promise made by the mayor. "He couldn't have been clearer about it, and he couldn't have been clearer about his interest in separating out First Amendment responsibility from counterterrorism responsibility. And that is something that I have long thought makes perfect sense. And so that's exactly what we've done here," Tisch said. Mamdani said the administration spent months developing the plan. "The reason we have taken 10 months to get to this point is to ensure that we could do so in a way that fulfilled the promise and was able to fulfill exactly those responsibilities that we hold," he said. The decision has drawn criticism from police unions . "When you are in policing, you got to be proactive, not reactive. And that's what's not happening now. Now we're going backwards," said Scott Munro of the Detectives Endowment Association The unit is scheduled to be dissolved in the spring of next year, when a new NYPD crowd-control unit will assume responsibility for facilitating nonviolent protests. ---------- * Get Eyewitness News Delivered * More New York City news * Send us a news tip * Download the abc7NY app for breaking news alerts * Follow us on YouTube Submit a tip or story idea to Eyewitness News Have a breaking news tip or an idea for a story we should cover? item.title: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
From grounded flights to frozen bank accounts , why does it seem like everything is breaking at once? First, millions of people lost access to their email . Next, the nation's skies went quiet. Then, a wave of customers trying to send money through Zelle were met with error messages. In just five days, a rapid succession of high-profile technology failures has left consumers rattled. The Federal Aviation Administration was forced into a rare nationwide ground stop. Microsoft’s ubiquitous office software went dark. Now a software bug has hit banking, and United Airlines had a fleeting system outage that delayed flight departures. Public anxiety coursed through social media. "So are we just pretending like it's normal that all of the mainstream banks are down today? After Microsoft? And planes? And..." one TikToker posted. "Can y'all wake me up when this timeline is over?" added another. The good news: No sign of a cyberattack First, the reassuring news. Patrick Moorhead, founder of Moor Insights and Strategy, says there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack and "nothing is falling apart." Instead, these compounding outages highlight a deeper structural vulnerability: How heavily our critical infrastructure relies on highly concentrated systems. "When one piece fails, it fails at national scale," Moorhead said. Modern technological systems are so complex and tightly interwoven that a single error can snowball instantly, wiping out essential services, according to Mike Chapple, a professor at the University of Notre Dame. The FAA outage, for example, was triggered by either a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project. That single mistake flooded the air traffic control network with data, crippling nationwide infrastructure, Chapple said. Meanwhile, the Microsoft outage was caused by a dormant software bug that had lingered undetected since July. Last week, "conditions were just right to activate the bug, triggering a cascade of failures that knocked thousands of systems offline and hindered repair efforts," he said. While the exact cause of the banking disruptions remains unclear, Chapple speculated it is likely a technical issue in shared payment networks. Chase said it experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug. The catch? Routine changes cause massive ripples American consumers are right to be frustrated, said Daniel Newman, CEO of Futurum Group. "Increasingly, there is a lack of clarity to consumers around why outages are happening and how they are being remedied," Newman said. Any vulnerability in these crucial systems is cause for major concern, says Mitch Ashley, vice president and practice lead at the Futurum Group. "Daily life runs on a small number of systems and a failure in one now reaches millions of people at once," he said. What's more, the recent spate of incidents while unrelated point to a common issue, said Virginia Tech professor Ali Butt. A "routine change" set each one off, he said. "Microsoft’s outage has been linked to a network configuration change and the FAA ground stop was traced to a maintenance upgrade on a single router. Imagine that, a single component in a sea of thousands or more components," Butt said. "In tightly connected systems, a small change made without fully mapping its downstream effects can spread far beyond where it started." Will outages get worse? Likely The bad news is that our dependence on massive-scale technology is only growing. Experts warn we should expect these failures to happen more often and hit harder. "Should people panic? No. Should we ask for better engineering? Yes," Butt said. "That means testing changes for their downstream impact, rolling them out in stages, isolating faults and setting clear policies for systems the public depends on."
